title: The hungry ghosts
hook: in Chinese communities, the seventh month's offerings to hungry ghosts and lost souls

segments.voice: Yesterday: Obon, welcome fires and the circle dance, and your line, they come home. Whose story did you tell? Today, a new week, and the guests nobody invites. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

Singapore, the seventh month of the lunar calendar. On the sidewalks, small fires burn in metal bins, paper offerings curling into ash. Little piles of oranges, rice and incense sit along the curbs. In open-air tents, singers perform loud, cheerful shows, and the front row of seats is left empty. Nobody sits there. Those seats, people say, are for the guests you can't see. Yesterday, Moggallana's mother was one hungry ghost, and her son could help her. In Chinese communities, this whole month is for all the others: the ghosts nobody remembers. Today: the hungry ghosts.
screen: `THE SEVENTH LUNAR MONTH.` → `OFFERINGS ON THE CURB.` → `THE EMPTY FRONT ROW.`

segments.voice: In Buddhist teaching, hungry ghosts, peta in Pali, preta in Sanskrit, are one of the realms of rebirth. Beings driven by craving so strong that nothing satisfies it. East Asian art pictures them with huge, empty bellies and throats as thin as a needle: always hungry, never able to swallow enough. The image is a teaching in itself. Craving, made visible. The Pali canon already speaks of them. A short text, the discourse outside the walls, pictures dead relatives standing outside houses, at crossroads and by doorposts, returning to their old homes, waiting. When the living give food and drink, and dedicate the merit to them, the ghosts rejoice. In China, these threads came together with older customs of honoring the dead. On the fifteenth night of the seventh month, Buddhist temples hold the Ullambana rites you heard about yesterday; Taoists keep the same night as the Zhongyuan festival. Often the two are woven together, and families may not draw a sharp line. In some temples, monks perform a ritual of feeding the hungry ghosts, scattering food and chanting so that it can reach beings who can't otherwise eat. Notice who the month is really for. Not your own grandparents only. The lost ones. Those who died far from home, or with no one left to remember them. The festival is a kind of public kindness toward strangers who can't say thank you.
screen: `PETA: ALWAYS HUNGRY.` · `HUGE BELLY, NEEDLE THROAT.` · `WAITING OUTSIDE THE WALLS.` · then, large: `FEED THE HUNGRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer food to someone hungry. Sit, and settle. First, notice hunger in yourself, any kind: for food, for attention, for something to be different. Don't judge it. Just see it, like the ghost's thin throat. Then widen out. Think of the hungry people near you, a shelter, a person on a corner, a neighbor stretched thin. Choose one way to feed someone today: a meal bought, a food bank gift, a plate shared. The bell holds the time.
The hungry ghosts. Peta, beings whose craving can never be satisfied, fed with offerings in the seventh lunar month in Chinese communities. Today's word.
Your line: feed the hungry. Today, feed someone who can't thank you, or give to a place that feeds strangers. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: In Chinese communities during the seventh lunar month, families make offerings of food, incense and paper goods, temples hold rites to feed hungry ghosts, and some communities stage performances with front-row seats left empty for unseen guests.

original.note: Pali peta (Sanskrit preta): 'departed one,' a hungry ghost, one of the realms of rebirth.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hungry ghost festival is about being scared of ghosts.
what it means: it's a month of feeding beings who are suffering and forgotten.
what a scholar hears: peta literally means 'departed,' one who has gone on; the Tirokudda text pictures these departed waiting by their old homes.

notes: Tirokudda Sutta paraphrased: confirm the walls, crossroads and doorposts, and the dedication of merit.
